subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Zabt system — features, regions and limitations

concepts.name: Zabt System: Definition and Structural Framework
key_dimensions: Etymology of 'Zabt' and its literal meaning (regulation/rule) vs. its administrative connotation
Distinction between Zabt as a measurement-based system vs. other revenue systems (Nasaq, Ghalla Bakshi)
Role of Todar Mal in formalizing and systematizing the Zabt system under Akbar
Zabt as a sub-category within the broader Dahsala (ten-year settlement) framework

concepts.name: Dahsala (Ten-Year Settlement) and its Relationship with Zabt
key_dimensions: How Dahsala averaged productivity and prices over 10 years to arrive at state demand
Common UPSC trap: Dahsala and Zabt are often conflated — Dahsala is the method of calculation; Zabt is the system of measurement and assessment
Role of Todar Mal in implementing Dahsala in 1580 CE and its geographic scope
Limitations of Dahsala: inability to reflect annual crop variations and local price fluctuations

concepts.name: Todar Mal's Role and Administrative Contribution to Revenue Reform
key_dimensions: Todar Mal's earlier service under Sher Shah Suri and continuity of revenue practices into Mughal period
Specific contributions: standardization of measurement (bigha), classification of land, creation of revenue records (khasra, khatauni)
Distinction between Todar Mal's reforms under Akbar vs. Sher Shah's earlier land revenue system
UPSC trap: Todar Mal vs. Raja Bhagwan Das — differentiating administrative roles

concepts.name: Land Classification under Zabt: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, Banjar
key_dimensions: Four-fold classification of land based on cultivation cycles and productivity
Polaj (continuously cultivated) vs. Parauti (temporarily fallow) vs. Chachar (3-4 years fallow) vs. Banjar (5+ years uncultivated)
Revenue implications: different assessment rates applied to each land category
UPSC trap: confusing Chachar and Banjar — distinguishing fallow duration and revenue treatment

concepts.name: Unit of Measurement: Ilahi Gaz and Bigha Standardization
key_dimensions: Introduction of the Ilahi Gaz (yard) as a standardized unit of measurement under Akbar
Variation in bigha sizes before standardization and the administrative problem this created
Relationship between standardized measurement and accurate assessment of cultivated area
UPSC trap: Ilahi Gaz vs. Sikandari Gaz — differentiating Mughal measurement standards

concepts.name: Schedule of Rates (Ain-i-Dahsala) and Crop-Wise Revenue Fixation
key_dimensions: How average prices of different crops over 10 years were recorded in the Ain-i-Dahsala
Crop-wise differentiation: revenue demand varied by crop type (food grains vs. cash crops)
State demand fixed at one-third of average produce — theoretical basis and actual practice
Significance of Ain-i-Akbari as a source for understanding schedule of rates

concepts.name: Geographic Regions Where Zabt Was Applied vs. Not Applied
key_dimensions: Zabt applied primarily in northern plains: Punjab, Agra, Allahabad, Awadh, Delhi, and parts of Malwa
Regions where Zabt was NOT applied: Bengal, Kashmir, Kabul, Orissa, and the Deccan — and the reasons why
Alternative systems in non-Zabt regions: Ghalla Bakshi (crop sharing) in Deccan and parts of Gujarat
UPSC trap: assuming Zabt was a pan-Mughal revenue system — it was geographically limited

concepts.name: Ghalla Bakshi (Batai) System: Features and Contrast with Zabt
key_dimensions: Ghalla Bakshi as a crop-sharing arrangement: state took a fixed share of actual produce
Three sub-types of Batai: Khet Batai (field division), Lang Batai (heap division), Raas Batai (threshed grain division)
Advantage over Zabt: more equitable in uncertain rainfall/crop areas; disadvantage: required state presence at harvest
Regions where Ghalla Bakshi was preferred over Zabt and why

concepts.name: Nasaq System: Features and Comparison with Zabt
key_dimensions: Nasaq as an empirical system based on past records and local agreements without fresh measurement
Nasaq as the dominant system in Bengal — its persistence despite Mughal attempts at standardization
Difference from Zabt: Zabt required fresh survey and measurement; Nasaq relied on estimated past yields
UPSC trap: Nasaq is sometimes described as a 'rough and ready' version of Zabt — identifying the key distinction

concepts.name: Role of Amil (Revenue Collector) and Local Administrative Machinery
key_dimensions: Functions of the Amil in supervising measurement, collection, and record-keeping at pargana level
Relationship between Amil, Qanungo (record-keeper), and Patwari (village accountant) in revenue hierarchy
Corruption and collusion at local level as a structural limitation of the Zabt system
UPSC trap: confusing Amil with Amalguzar — both are revenue officials but at different hierarchical levels

concepts.name: Qanungo and Patwari: Record-Keeping Infrastructure of Zabt
key_dimensions: Qanungo as the hereditary record-keeper at pargana level — custodian of revenue records
Patwari as village-level accountant responsible for maintaining khasra (field register)
Importance of written records (khasra, khatauni, jamabandi) in making Zabt a systematic revenue tool
Limitation: records were often manipulated by local intermediaries, undermining the system's accuracy

concepts.name: Limitations of Zabt: Practical and Structural Failures
key_dimensions: Assumption of fixed prices and yields did not account for annual variations, droughts, or famines
System was inequitable in rain-fed (barani) areas vs. irrigated (abi) areas — same rates applied differently
High transaction costs: extensive survey and measurement required large administrative machinery
Peasant resistance and evasion: under-reporting of cultivated area, collusion with local officials

concepts.name: Zabt and the Jagirdari System: Structural Tension
key_dimensions: Jagirdars assigned revenue from specific territories — their interest in maximizing extraction clashed with standardized Zabt rates
Zabt theoretically protected peasants from arbitrary extraction; in practice, jagirdars often exceeded assessed demand
Concept of 'jama' (assessed revenue) vs. 'hasil' (actual collection) — persistent gap between the two
UPSC trap: assuming Zabt automatically restrained jagirdari exploitation — the gap between theory and practice

concepts.name: Jama-Hasil Gap: Assessed Revenue vs. Actual Collection
key_dimensions: Jama as the theoretically assessed demand under Zabt; Hasil as actual revenue realized
Chronic Jama-Hasil gap as evidence of Zabt's implementation failures
Irfan Habib's analysis of the Jama-Hasil ratio as an indicator of agrarian stress under Mughals
Implications for peasant indebtedness and eventual agrarian crisis in late Mughal period

concepts.name: Zabt and Cash vs. Kind Payment: Monetization of Agrarian Economy
key_dimensions: Zabt calculated revenue in cash (dams/rupees), pushing peasants toward market participation
Role of Zabt in accelerating monetization of the agrarian economy in northern India
Problem of market access for peasants in remote areas — forced distress sales to meet cash demand
Irfan Habib's argument that cash revenue demand was a driver of peasant indebtedness and revolts

concepts.name: Zabt under Later Mughals: Decline and Distortion
key_dimensions: Progressive weakening of Zabt implementation after Aurangzeb due to jagirdari crisis and administrative decay
How expansion into Deccan overstretched the Mughal revenue machinery, making Zabt unworkable in new territories
Rise of revenue farming (ijaradari) as a substitute when Zabt could no longer be maintained
UPSC trap: assuming Zabt continued uniformly throughout Mughal rule — it was strongest under Akbar-Jahangir period

concepts.name: Influence of Sher Shah Suri's Revenue System on Zabt
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's earlier land survey, measurement standardization, and schedule of rates as precursor to Mughal Zabt
Continuity vs. innovation: what Akbar adopted from Sher Shah and what was distinctly Mughal
Todar Mal's service under Sher Shah as the biographical link between the two systems
UPSC trap: attributing all revenue innovations to Akbar — recognizing Sher Shah's foundational contribution

concepts.name: Zabt System in Historiography: Irfan Habib vs. Other Historians
key_dimensions: Irfan Habib's 'The Agrarian System of Mughal India' as the foundational scholarly work on Zabt
Habib's thesis: Zabt-driven cash revenue demand led to peasant exploitation and agrarian crises
Alternative views: Shireen Moosvi's quantitative analysis suggesting Mughal peasants retained a reasonable share
UPSC angle: source-based questions may draw on Ain-i-Akbari descriptions of Zabt — identifying Abul Fazl as the primary source

concepts.name: Ain-i-Akbari as a Source for Zabt: Content and Limitations
key_dimensions: Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari (part of Akbarnama) as the primary Mughal source detailing Zabt procedures
Ain-i-Akbari's schedule of prices, yields, and revenue rates — its use by historians to reconstruct Mughal agrarian economy
Limitations of Ain-i-Akbari as a source: it reflects official/ideal conditions, not ground realities
UPSC trap: treating Ain-i-Akbari as an objective record — recognizing it as a court-commissioned, celebratory document

concepts.name: Zabt and Its Impact on Peasant (Raiyat) Rights and Conditions
key_dimensions: Whether Zabt gave peasants any legal security of tenure — concept of 'occupancy rights' in Mughal period
Distinction between peasant rights under Zabt theory vs. actual conditions of eviction and mobility
Role of zamindars as intermediaries between state/Zabt system and the actual cultivating peasant
Debate on whether Mughal peasants were 'serfs' or 'free peasants' — Irfan Habib's position and its critics
